name: Chlorodehydromethyltestosterone (Turinabol / Oral Turinabol)

lead: Turinabol is an oral anabolic steroid, a chlorinated version of metandienone, known for its place in East Germany's state doping programme. Lifters favour it for lean, dry-looking muscle with less water retention.

It activates the androgen receptor, which raises muscle protein gain. It was in clinical use from 1965 to 1994, and its long-lasting urinary metabolites, identified in 2012, allowed old Olympic samples to be re-tested. Published research is mostly metabolism and detection studies, plus isolated case reports of harm.

paras: People use it as a tablet taken by mouth in cycles alongside heavy training and a calorie surplus or cut, often stacked with other compounds. Lifters describe gains building over several weeks.

Documented harms are limited to case reports and general anabolic-steroid concerns, including liver strain, hormone suppression and a case report of a testicular tumour after high-dose use. It is banned in sport and controlled in the US, UK and Brazil.

angle.text: Turinabol is an oral steroid used for lean, dry muscle gain: it activates the androgen receptor, speeding muscle protein gain with little water retention. Its history and detection science are well documented, while clinical trials for muscle or appearance have not been published.

lead: Chlorodehydromethyltestosterone (CDMT, DHCMT), sold as Oral-Turinabol and nicknamed Tbol, is an oral anabolic-androgenic steroid, the 4-chloro derivative of metandienone. It was the first original product of the East German pharmaceutical company Jenapharm, patented in 1961, introduced clinically in 1965 and discontinued in 1994 [1].

It is best known as the central drug in East Germany's state doping programme, which according to Wikipedia ran from about 1968 to 1989 and involved thousands of athletes [1]. Long-lasting urinary metabolites identified in 2012 allowed retrospective re-testing of stored Olympic samples [1].
Published clinical research on Oral-Turinabol as a treatment is scarce. The literature consists largely of metabolism and detection studies, plus isolated case reports of harm.
infobox: US Schedule III; UK Class C; Brazil Class C5; WADA-prohibited

paras: Wikipedia reports that chemist Albert Stachowiak proposed combining the structures of clostebol and metandienone, producing a compound that became Jenapharm's first original product [1]. After its clinical introduction in 1965, it became the main steroid in a secret state-run doping programme (State Plan Topic 14.25), with athletes often given tablets described to them as vitamins [1]. Researchers Franke and Berendonk documented the programme from East German archives in the 1990s [1]. Later, the IOC re-analysed stored samples from the 2008 and 2012 Games using a method for long-term CDMT metabolites and reported positives among weightlifters and sprinters [1].

Human metabolism of Oral-Turinabol yields hydroxylated metabolites that are detectable in urine [2]. Studies have examined how human steroidogenic cytochrome P450 enzymes metabolise it [3] and have synthesised long-term metabolites for use as anti-doping reference material [4]. Wikipedia gives an elimination half-life of about 16 hours, but this figure is tagged as needing a citation [1].

No studies found of Oral-Turinabol for appearance or physique. Human-related literature consists of metabolite identification [2][3][4] and a case report of an intratesticular leiomyosarcoma in a 32-year-old man after high-dose doping with the drug, in which the authors raised a possible but unproven association [5]. Animal work on anabolic steroids more broadly has reported effects on the heart, such as impaired growth of the cardiac capillary bed in exercise-trained animals [6].

The drug remains prohibited in sport. Wikipedia lists high-profile doping cases involving turinabol, including mixed martial artist Jon Jones after UFC 214 in 2017 and baseball player Colton Welker in 2021 [1]. In bodybuilding circles it is described under the nickname Tbol as an oral steroid associated with its East German history, though no published trials test those claims.
